newsitem.title: FRANCE: French Communists bosses want to join government.
newsitem.headline: French Communists bosses want to join government.

text.p: France's Communist Party bosses on Tuesday recommended joining a Socialist-led government after the party came back from the cold in France's parliamentary election to win the balance of power in the National Assembly.

The party's policy-making national committee, which opposes a single European Union currency and wants wage increases for the lowest-paid, said the Socialists had "satisfactorily" taken Communist views into account in defining the new government's policies.

"The national committee proposes...to reply positively to the question of participation in a leftist parliamentary majority and to that of Communist ministers in the French government," a party statement said.

The recommendation would be put to grassroots members, who have never defied their leaders, later on Tuesday. A final decision would be made on Wednesday at a national committee meeting starting at 10 a.m. (0800 GMT).

The Communist party won 38 of 577 National Assembly seats in Sunday's parliamentary election, giving it the balance of power. The non-Communist left won 274 seats -- short of the 289 needed for a majority.

The statement did not spell out any conditions as the price for joining Socialist Prime Minister Lionel Jospin's government, merely saying it wanted clear signs that the Socialists would carry through pledges of change.

Jospin repeatedly said during the campaign that leftists wanting to take part in a Socialist-led government would have to bow to the Socialist line. Unlike the Communists, the Socialists broadly favour the euro single currency.

Communist Party boss Robert Hue spoke to Jospin on Tuesday and reiterated demands for an immediate increase in the minimum monthly wage, a two percentage point cut in general value added tax and bigger cuts in VAT on basic products.
Hue said on Monday that the national committee had agreed in principle that Communists should serve in the new government as long as policy questions could be resolved.
Jospin aides have said that the Communists may get two ministries and one post of secretary of state.
The party was last in government under late president Francois Mitterrand, from 1981 to 1984. It held the balance of power when a Socialist-led government ruled from 1988 to 1993.

On Monday, grassroots communists in the Val-de-Marne area, a bastion of former hardline party leader Georges Marchais who approved the 1979 Soviet invasion of Afghanistan, voted by 88 percent to take part in government.

The Socialists and Communists signed a pre-election declaration outlining plans to cut the working week to 35 hours from 39 and to create 700,000 youth jobs. But the Communists want both measures implemented far faster than the Socialists.

Jack Ralite, a former health minister and junior minister for employment in 1981-84, urged the Communists to take part in government. "People are drowning, the Communist Party should roll up its sleeves and do the dirty work," he said.

The 1992 Maastricht Treaty set a course for deeper European political and monetary union, including strict terms for a country's qualification for the euro single currency, due to be launched in 1999.
